questions.q: In the lab scenario, what exactly was broken after the approval-routing feature went live?
options: Approval records stopped being created entirely
The approval workflow itself was fully broken for every request
Approvals were still processing correctly, but the notification email alerting department heads to a pending approval wasn't sending for requests that hit the new step
The Equipment Checkout application went completely offline
questions.explain: The underlying workflow logic was sound — the gap was narrower: a silent notification failure, not a broken approval process.

questions.q: What was the actual root cause the team found in the notification script?
options: The script had no null check for the department head field, which could legitimately be empty for some newer request types, causing the notification to silently fail
The script was deleted during the deployment
The department head field was renamed and no longer existed
The notification script was never deployed to Production
questions.explain: A missing null check let an empty field silently stop the notification from sending, with no visible error to anyone.

questions.q: Why did the team choose roll forward instead of a full revert?
options: Reverting is always faster than rolling forward, regardless of circumstances

The issue was moderate (not widespread catastrophic failure), the root cause was precisely identified, and reverting would have removed the legitimate second-approval requirement entirely, re-opening a compliance gap
A revert was technically impossible for this application
The team flipped a coin between the two options
questions.explain: Applying Lesson 22's criteria: moderate severity, a known precise root cause, and a revert that would cost more (losing the compliance control) than it would save.

questions.q: What planning gap from Lesson 21 actually caused this incident to become a live, business-hours problem?
options: The feature was deployed out of dependency sequence
The deployment went live at 10:30 AM on a business day instead of inside a planned maintenance window, so the bug was discovered by confused employees in real time
The team never ran any Automated Test Framework tests
The CAB rejected the change but it was deployed anyway
questions.explain: The bug itself was a code defect, not a scheduling conflict — but deploying during business hours is why it became a live incident instead of a quiet fix.

questions.q: What is the lab's closing point about planning and rollback?
options: A good rollback decision limits the damage from a planning mistake, but it doesn't erase it — planning and rollback are not separate, unrelated skills
Rollback decisions make deployment planning unnecessary
Once a rollback is executed correctly, the original planning mistake no longer matters at all
Planning only matters if the rollback decision turns out to be wrong
questions.explain: The technical fix resolved the symptom, but the real lesson is upstream: the timing mistake from Lesson 21 is what turned a moderate bug into a live incident.
